content: 1. Zanamivir has been evaluated for its efficacy in chemoprophylaxis against influenza A and B in populations requiring complex continuing care. (Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol, 2002; 23(10):604-8). 2. A systematic review by Jefferson et al. analyzed the effectiveness of antiviral medications in healthy adults for the treatment of influenza. (Lancet, 2006; 367(9507):303-13). 3. Jefferson and colleagues also reviewed the use of amantadine and rimantadine for the treatment of influenza A in adults, providing insights into their clinical applications. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2006(2):CD001169). 4. Bhat et al. investigated influenza-associated deaths among children in the United States during the 2003-2004 season, highlighting the significant impact of influenza on pediatric populations. (N Engl J Med, 2005; 353(24):2559-67). 5. Cheung et al. demonstrated the effectiveness of noninvasive positive pressure ventilation in managing acute respiratory failure in patients with severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS). (Chest, 2004; 126(3):845-50). 6. Christian et al. explored the potential transmission of SARS coronavirus during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, emphasizing the need for infection control measures. (Emerg Infect Dis, 2004; 10(2):287-93). 7. Wan et al. concluded that large-volume nebulizers are unlikely to serve as infectious sources for SARS, based on their study. (Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol, 2004; 25(12):1113-5). 8. Somogyi et al. examined the dispersal of respiratory droplets with open versus closed oxygen delivery masks, discussing implications for SARS transmission. (Chest, 2004; 125(3):1155-7). 9. Hui et al. studied airflow patterns around oxygen masks, raising concerns about their potential role as sources of infection. (Chest, 2006; 130(3):822-6). 10. Harrel and Molinari reviewed the generation of aerosols and splatter in dentistry, discussing their implications for infection control. (J Am Dent Assoc, 2004; 135(4):429-37). 11. Catanzaro and Jackson provided guidance on preventing nosocomial transmission of tuberculosis, emphasizing the importance of infection control practices. (Lancet, 1995; 345(8944):204-5). 12. Malasky et al. reported on occupational tuberculosis infections among pulmonary physicians in training, highlighting the risks associated with clinical exposure. (Am Rev Respir Dis, 1990; 142(3):505-7). 13. Nogler et al. investigated environmental and body contamination caused by aerosols generated during lumbar spine surgery using high-speed cutters. (Spine, 2001; 26(19):2156-9). 14. Nogler et al. also studied the extent of environmental contamination from aerosols produced during cervical spine surgery. (Eur Spine J, 2001; 10(4):274-7). 15. Burton discussed health and safety considerations during necropsy, focusing on infection risks and preventive measures. (J Clin Pathol, 2003; 56(4):254-60). 16. Beggs et al. reviewed the transmission of tuberculosis in confined spaces, analyzing various epidemiological models. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis, 2003; 7(11):1015-26). 17. Mehta et al. provided a consensus statement on preventing infections associated with flexible bronchoscopy, emphasizing best practices. (Chest, 2005; 128(3):1742-55). 18. Yu et al. investigated why SARS outbreaks occurred in some hospital wards but not others, identifying key factors influencing transmission. (Clin Infect Dis, 2007; 44(8):1017-25). 19. Loeb et al. reported on SARS cases among critical care nurses in Toronto, highlighting occupational risks. (Emerg Infect Dis, 2004; 10(2):251-5). 20. Cooper et al. outlined practical approaches to airway management in patients with SARS, addressing challenges in critical care. (CMAJ, 2003; 169(8):785-7). 21. Pippin et al. evaluated the efficacy of face masks in preventing inhalation of airborne contaminants, providing evidence for their protective role. (J Oral Maxillofac Surg, 1987; 45(4):319-23). 22. Kaye et al. discussed nosocomial infections associated with respiratory therapy, emphasizing the importance of proper equipment disinfection. (Hospital Epidemiology and Infection Control, 3rd ed., 2004:1207-22). 23. Derrick and Gomersall assessed the filtration capacity of multiple surgical masks in protecting healthcare staff from SARS. (J Hosp Infect, 2005; 59(4):365-8). 24. Lenhart et al. addressed issues affecting respirator selection for workers exposed to infectious aerosols, with a focus on healthcare settings. (Applied Biosafety, 2004; 9(1):20-36). 25. Allard and Santamouris edited a handbook on natural ventilation in buildings, providing design guidelines for improved airflow. (1998). 26. Liddament authored a guide on energy-efficient ventilation, offering practical solutions for building design. (1996). 27. Awbi published a second edition on building ventilation, discussing principles and applications for maintaining indoor air quality. (2003). 28. Li and Delsante studied natural ventilation induced by combined wind and thermal forces, contributing to building environment research. (Building and Environment, 2001; 36:59-71). 29. Irving et al. developed an inverse solver for sizing passive ventilation openings, advancing computational methods in ventilation design. (1995). 30. Axley introduced the design of natural ventilation systems using loop equations, presented at the 19th AIVC Conference. (1998). 31. Fanger analyzed thermal comfort and its applications in environmental engineering, providing foundational knowledge. (1970). 32. Brady et al. examined the survival and disinfection of parainfluenza viruses on environmental surfaces, informing infection control practices. (Am J Infect Control, 1990; 18(1):18-23). 33. Suarez et al. evaluated the effects of various disinfectants on detecting avian influenza virus using real-time RT-PCR. (Avian Dis, 2003; 47(3 Suppl):1091-5). 34. Sattar et al. studied chemical disinfection to interrupt rhinovirus transfer from surfaces to hands, emphasizing hygiene practices. (Appl Environ Microbiol, 1993; 59(5):1579-85). 35. Sattar et al. also investigated the disinfection of non-porous surfaces contaminated with human pathogenic viruses. (Epidemiol Infect, 1989; 102(3):493-505). 36. Rabeneau et al. evaluated the efficacy of various disinfectants against SARS coronavirus, providing evidence for infection control. (J Hosp Infect, 2005; 61(2):107-11). 37. Dettenkofer et al. conducted a systematic review on whether environmental surface disinfection influences nosocomial infection rates. (Am J Infect Control, 2004; 32(2):84-9). 38. Scott and Bloomfield investigated the effectiveness of detergent washing, drying, and chemical disinfection on cleaning cloth contamination. (J Appl Bacteriol, 1990; 68(3):279-83). 39. Medcraft et al. highlighted potential hazards from spray cleaning hospital floors, emphasizing the need for safe cleaning practices. (J Hosp Infect, 1987; 9(2):151-7). 40. Spaulding discussed chemical disinfection of medical and surgical materials, providing a comprehensive overview. (1968). 41. Rutala provided APIC guidelines for selecting and using disinfectants, offering practical recommendations for healthcare settings. (Am J Infect Control, 1996; 24(4):313-42). 42. Cefai et al. reported an outbreak of Acinetobacter respiratory tract infections due to incomplete disinfection of ventilatory equipment. (J Hosp Infect, 1990; 15(2):177-82). 43. Craven et al. identified contaminated medication nebulizers in ventilator circuits as sources of bacterial aerosols. (Am J Med, 1984; 77(5):834-8). 44. Spach et al. reviewed infection transmission via gastrointestinal endoscopy and bronchoscopy, emphasizing the need for stringent disinfection. (Ann Intern Med, 1993; 118(2):117-28). 45. Weber and Rutala analyzed lessons from outbreaks associated with bronchoscopy, highlighting infection control failures. (Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol, 2001; 22(7):403-8). 46. Wheeler et al. investigated bronchopulmonary cross-colonization and infection related to mycobacterial contamination of bronchoscope suction valves. (J Infect Dis, 1989; 159(5):954-8). 47. Poledore studied the sanitizing efficiency of dishwashing machines, providing insights into their role in infection control. (J Foodservice, 1980). 48. Stahl Wernersson et al. examined cross-contamination in dishwashers, emphasizing the importance of proper cleaning protocols. (J Hosp Infect, 2004; 56(4):312-7). 49. Ijaz et al. evaluated the effects of relative humidity, temperature, and suspending medium on the airborne survival of human rotavirus. (Can J Microbiol, 1985; 31(8):681-5). 50. Marks et al. provided evidence for airborne transmission of Norwalk-like virus in a hotel restaurant outbreak. (Epidemiol Infect, 2000; 124(3):481-7). 51. Marks et al. also documented a school outbreak of Norwalk-like virus, supporting airborne transmission as a mode of spread. (Epidemiol Infect, 2003; 131(1):727-36). 52. Battles and Vesley studied wash water temperature and sanitation in hospital laundry, emphasizing its role in infection control. (J Environ Health, 1981; 43(5):244-50). 53. Blaser et al. investigated the killing of fabric-associated bacteria in hospital laundry using low-temperature washing. (J Infect Dis, 1984; 149(1):48-57). 54. Christian et al. assessed the bacteriological quality of fabrics washed at lower-than-standard temperatures in hospital laundry facilities. (Appl Environ Microbiol, 1983; 45(2):591-7). 55. Barker and Jones explored the potential spread of infection caused by aerosol contamination of surfaces after flushing a domestic toilet. (J Appl Microbiol, 2005; 99(2):339-47). 56. Morawska discussed the fate of droplets in indoor environments and strategies to prevent the spread of infection. (Indoor Air, 2006; 16(5):335-47). 57. Karanfil et al. described strategies for reducing nosocomial transmission of respiratory syncytial virus. (Am J Infect Control, 1999; 27(2):91-6). 58. Mlinaric-Galinovic and Varda-Brkic reported on nosocomial respiratory syncytial virus infections in children's wards. (Diagn Microbiol Infect Dis, 2000; 37(4):237-46). 59. Thorburn et al. documented an RSV outbreak in a pediatric intensive care unit, emphasizing the need for infection control measures. (J Hosp Infect, 2004; 57(3):194-201). 60. Ibricevic et al. studied influenza virus receptor specificity and cell tropism in mouse and human airway epithelial cells. (J Virol, 2006; 80(15):7469-80). 61. The CDC issued guidelines for preventing the transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in healthcare facilities in 1994 and updated them in 2005. (MMWR, 1994; 43(RR-13):1-132; 2005; 54(RR-17)). 62. Le et al. reported a lack of SARS transmission among public hospital workers in Vietnam, highlighting effective infection control practices. (Emerg Infect Dis, 2004; 10(2):265-8). 63. Park et al. similarly documented a lack of SARS transmission among healthcare workers in the United States. (Emerg Infect Dis, 2004; 10(2):244-8). 64. Peck et al. described a SARS case-patient, providing insights into clinical and epidemiological aspects. (Emerg Infect Dis, 2004; 10(2):217-24). 65. Ali et al. reviewed the use of alcohols as disinfectants, discussing their applications in healthcare settings. (Disinfection, Sterilization, and Preservation, 5th ed., 2000:229-53). 66. Bell analyzed public health interventions and their impact on the spread of SARS in 2003. (Emerg Infect Dis, 2004; 10(11):1900-6). 67. Rutala et al. evaluated the efficacy of a washer-pasteurizer for disinfecting respiratory-care equipment. (Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol, 2000; 21(5):333-6). 68. Gillis and Rennick emphasized the importance of affirming parental love in the pediatric intensive care unit. (Pediatr Crit Care Med, 2006; 7(2):165-8). 69. Leidy et al. examined the impact of severe respiratory syncytial virus on children, caregivers, and families during hospitalization and recovery. (Pediatrics, 2005; 115(6):1536-46). 70. Hanrahan and Lofgren reviewed the risks associated with toys in the microenvironment of infants in neonatal intensive care units. (Adv Neonatal Care, 2004; 4(4):184-201). 71. Avila-Aguero et al. investigated whether toys in pediatric hospitals serve as bacterial sources. (Am J Infect Control, 2004; 32(5):287-90). 72. Buttery et al. reported a multiresistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa outbreak in a pediatric oncology ward linked to bath toys. (Pediatr Infect Dis J, 1998; 17(6):509-13). 73. Davies et al. studied bacterial colonization of toys in neonatal intensive care cots, emphasizing the need for proper cleaning. (Pediatrics, 2000; 106(2):E18). 74. Hick et al. discussed healthcare facility and community strategies for managing patient care surge capacity. (Ann Emerg Med, 2004; 44(3):253-61). 75. Hogg et al. proposed increasing epidemic surge capacity through home-based hospital care. (Can Fam Physician, 2006; 52:563-4, 570-2). 76. Martin addressed concerns about avian flu in home healthcare settings, providing guidance for preparedness. (Home Healthc Nurse, 2006; 24(1):38-45).
